title: Jumping to Conclusions About People
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines the habit of jumping to conclusions about other people's motives, feelings, or talent, and how it quietly damages relationships and decisions. It shows how a leader's snap assumption, such as believing a colleague expects to fail, can trigger a self-fulfilling cycle of defensiveness and conflict on both sides. The piece extends the pattern to hiring, where fast, confident first impressions can pollute a whole team's ability to judge a candidate objectively. It argues that people who jump to conclusions rarely audit their own track record, which is why they keep trusting their gut, and recommends deliberately asking more questions before forming a judgment.
points: Jumping to conclusions about people is based on limited information and often leads to poor choices.
A leader's false assumption about a colleague's mindset can trigger real defensiveness and conflict.
Believing you can read others' minds or predict relationships is a common but risky trap.
Snap judgments about job candidates can bias the whole hiring team's perception.
Those who jump to conclusions rarely examine their own track record, reinforcing the habit.
Asking more questions before judging is the main defense against this distortion.
quotes: Leaders who jump to conclusions about others make fast assumptions on limited information.
Acting defensive when others have no idea why is more than just irritating and annoying; indeed, it commonly produces equal defensiveness from the other party.
True mind-readers and fortunetellers are in short supply, so when a leader believes they have an inside edge, they are likely wrong.
Once they jump to a conclusion and become outspoken about a prospective candidate, their view pollutes the ability of others to make objective judgments, as well.
Perhaps the only way to curtail the cognitive distortion of jumping to conclusions is to encourage jumpers to ask more questions before making split-second judgments.
